analysis.one_liner: Caps attorneys' fees and adds loser-pays rules in lawsuits against gun makers and dealers.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in March 2002 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targeted lawsuits filed against firearms manufacturers, importers, and dealers seeking large damages for harms caused when someone else misused a gun. It would cap the winning side's lawyers' fees at $150 an hour or 10 percent of any award, require plaintiffs to pay the gun company's legal bills if the company was found not fully liable, and let any court ruling against Congress's power to pass the law go straight to the Supreme Court. It would have applied to lawsuits already underway. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_benefits: Firearms manufacturers, importers, and dealers facing city and county lawsuits over gun violence. The fee cap and mandatory reimbursement would sharply raise the cost and risk of suing them, deterring suits even where they might otherwise settle or lose. [S3]

how_it_helps.text: It caps plaintiff attorneys' fees in covered lawsuits at the lesser of $150 per hour plus expenses or 10 percent of any recovery, even overriding private fee agreements. [S3]

It requires plaintiffs to reimburse the defendant gun company's attorney fees and court costs whenever the court finds the defendant is not wholly or primarily liable, unless special circumstances make that unjust. [S3]

It covers lawsuits seeking more than $1 million (or half a defendant's net assets) to hold a gun company liable for unlawful or tortious use of a firearm by someone unaffiliated with the company — the theory behind municipal suits against gun makers. [S2] [S3]
It applies to any action pending or on appeal on the date of enactment, not just future suits. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Plaintiffs in gun lawsuits — crime victims' families and local governments seeking damages — and their lawyers, who would face capped fees and the risk of paying the gun company's legal bills. Gun-violence victims generally would lose a legal avenue for holding manufacturers accountable. [S2] [S3]

drawbacks.text: The fee cap applies even when the plaintiff and attorney privately agreed to a different arrangement, and courts must order plaintiffs to pay the gun company's legal costs in any case where the company is found not wholly or primarily liable — a rule that could deter validly supported suits against a manufacturer sharing only part of the blame. [S3]
Supporters would have to acknowledge the bill applies retroactively to lawsuits already in progress, changing the rules mid-case for cities and victims already suing. [S3]

The bill's core effect is to make it harder to recover damages in court for harm caused by guns, which backers of such suits argued was the point — raising litigation costs until manufacturers changed sales practices. [S2] [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the gun industry, the bill offered strong protection from costly litigation, and its findings frame that as protecting small businesses and the Second Amendment. The cost falls on plaintiffs — including victims and local governments — whose ability to use litigation to shift gun-industry conduct would be narrowed, and the fee cap even overrides private attorney-client agreements, a departure from normal contract freedom. Whether that trade is worth it depends on whether one views these lawsuits as accountability or as attrition warfare against a lawful industry; the bill picks the latter view and writes it into federal law. [S3]

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Sen. Bob Smith introduced the bill on March 7, 2002, with two Republican cosponsors. [S1] [S4]
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day. [S1] [S5]
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, no committee report, no floor vote — before the 107th Congress ended. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearms manufacturers lost a chance at litigation protection, while cities and plaintiffs retained their ability to sue gun companies under existing law. The bill's death left the legal status quo intact.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun-suit plaintiffs kept the status quo

for.name: Bob Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited two Senate cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: Only three Republican senators sponsored the bill and there was no recorded vote or committee action, so the partisan shape of broader support and opposition never showed itself. [S4] [S5]

industries.note: The bill would have sharply limited their exposure to large-damage lawsuits over gun misuse by third parties, by capping plaintiff fees and forcing plaintiffs to pay their legal costs. That protection comes at the expense of victims and local governments using litigation to change industry conduct. [S3]
A fee cap of $150 per hour or 10 percent of recovery, plus mandatory fee reimbursement to defendants, would make these suits financially risky and largely unprofitable. [S3]
The bill's findings directly target municipal lawsuits against gun makers, and the loser-pays provision would expose cities to paying manufacturers' legal costs when a suit fell short. [S3]
